lesson.child_mission: Area problems ask how much covering is needed, how many tiles fit, or what missing side makes a given area.
lesson.evidence_instructions: Save the independent response, specific revisions and both short-answer explanations; record oral evidence for speaking tasks.
lesson.extension: Apply the same method to a larger number or a new context, then compare two solution paths for accuracy.
lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
A rectangle area is 36 cm² and length 9 cm. Find the width. How many 1 cm² tiles cover it?

FEEDBACK
Width 4 cm; 36 tiles.

WATCH FOR
Using perimeter when the story is about covering solves the wrong problem.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Solve eight area word problems (tiling, covering, missing side). Sketch each rectangle and show the multiplication.

Write a short reflection naming one step you corrected and why.
lesson.learning_intention: Area problems ask how much covering is needed, how many tiles fit, or what missing side makes a given area.
materials: Optional: place-value chart or number line
lesson.offline_alternative: Use paper and pencil to complete the original task, then retain a photograph or short parent observation as evidence.
lesson.parent_notes:
Parent: Marking guidance for the independent task: Solve eight area word problems (tiling, covering, missing side). Sketch each rectangle and show the multiplication. Accept equivalent original responses that show the same skill.

Parent: Written model 1: Original demonstration: A patio 3 m by 4 m needs area 12 m² of tiles. If area is 24 cm² and width 4 cm, length=6 cm because 4×6=24.

Parent: Written model 2: Common error: Using perimeter when the story is about covering solves the wrong problem. Correction: Width 4 cm; 36 tiles.

Parent: Likely misconception: Using perimeter when the story is about covering solves the wrong problem. Keep sample answers out of the child role.

teach_steps.explain:
Area problems ask how much covering is needed, how many tiles fit, or what missing side makes a given area.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner choose methods based on place value, quantity and accurate working, rather than guessing digits by shape alone. Keep every step justified.

HOW TO WORK
Read the worked example and name the places, values or distances that carry the method. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. Compare your working with the feedback: did you use the same skill and show your reasoning? If a digit or place is uncertain, identify what would have to be regrouped or counted again. One deliberate, justified revision is more useful than writing a longer answer.
